card.chief_complaint: new periumbilical pain now in left lower quadrant

ask.changes_what: Migration present: treat as likely appendicitis, obtain imaging or surgical review; absent: keep appendicitis on the differential but weigh alternatives.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of migration to exclude appendicitis in young children, the elderly, pregnancy or patients with unreliable histories.
ask.escalation_warning: Migration followed by sudden generalised pain and rigidity suggests perforation: urgent surgical review.

evidence.citation: Benabbas R, Hanna M, Shah J, Sinert R. Diagnostic Accuracy of History, Physical Examination, Laboratory Tests, and Point-of-care Ultrasound for Pediatric Acute Appendicitis in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2017;24(5):523-551.
evidence.population: ED pediatric patients with undifferentiated abdominal pain; pooled from included studies (systematic review of 21 studies, 8605 patients overall)
evidence.quote: history of "pain migration to right lower quadrant (RLQ)" (LR+ = 4.81, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.59-6.44)
evidence.reference_standard: Surgical pathology or clinical follow-up as defined per study

ask.how: Ask where the pain started and where it is now, and in what order symptoms appeared. Migration means a vague periumbilical or epigastric (visceral) pain that, over hours, shifts to a sharper localised RLQ (parietal) pain; also ask whether pain preceded vomiting and about anorexia.
ask.negative_finding: Lack of migration makes appendicitis less likely but many confirmed cases present with RLQ pain from the outset, so absence does not exclude it.
ask.pitfalls: Migration is reported in only about half of cases and is recalled unreliably; retrocaecal or pelvic appendices localise atypically. Vomiting before pain onset argues against appendicitis.
ask.positive_finding: Classic periumbilical-to-RLQ migration raises the probability of appendicitis (pediatric pooled LR+ 4.8 in undifferentiated abdominal pain; adult OR 2.2), more than RLQ pain alone.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; for children or cognitively impaired patients, use carer history.
ask.title: Right lower quadrant pain with periumbilical-to-RLQ migration

ask.changes_what: With distension/vomiting: lowers threshold for CT and NG decompression. No prior surgery with SBO features: expect non-adhesive cause and earlier surgical involvement.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not let a prior-surgery history anchor the diagnosis on adhesions when signs of strangulation, hernia, or malignancy are present; do not dismiss SBO in a patient without prior surgery.
ask.escalation_warning: SBO features with fever, tachycardia, peritonism or lactate rise indicate strangulation: fluids, antibiotics, immediate surgical consultation regardless of adhesion history.
ask.how: Ask specifically about any previous abdominal or pelvic operation (including laparoscopic, gynecologic, hernia repair and appendicectomy), radiotherapy, and prior episodes of obstruction; inspect for scars, which patients may not mention.
ask.negative_finding: A 'virgin abdomen' makes adhesive SBO much less likely and shifts the differential toward hernia, malignancy, volvulus, Crohn's or gallstone ileus, which more often need operation.
ask.pitfalls: Patients forget minor or remote procedures; laparoscopy and pelvic surgery also cause adhesions. The item is a risk factor, not a diagnostic sign, and most patients with scars presenting with pain do not have SBO.
ask.positive_finding: Prior laparotomy is the dominant risk factor for adhesive small bowel obstruction; in the OMGE series it was the most efficient historical item (RR 12.1) and is one of the best history predictors in the 2013 meta-analysis.
ask.prerequisites: None; corroborate with old records or inspection of the abdomen.
ask.title: History of prior abdominal surgery (adhesion risk)

ask.changes_what: Present: check lipase and consider pancreatitis, but exclude aortic catastrophe and perforation first when the patient is unstable or the pain is tearing/sudden.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not label pain as pancreatitis when there is hypotension, syncope, a pulsatile mass, limb ischemia or a tearing quality until aorta is imaged.
ask.escalation_warning: Epigastric pain to the back with shock, peritonitis, or a normal lipase demands urgent CT for aortic rupture, dissection or perforated viscus.
ask.how: Ask onset, location, and character: constant severe epigastric or upper-abdominal pain, often boring through to the back, worse supine and eased by sitting forward, with nausea and vomiting. Ask about alcohol intake, known gallstones or prior biliary colic, recent ERCP, hypertriglyceridemia and new medications.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of back radiation does not exclude pancreatitis; pain that is intermittent or colicky favours biliary colic or bowel pathology.
ask.pitfalls: Tearing pain with pulse or BP asymmetry, hypotension or a pulsatile mass points to aorta, not pancreas; elderly and post-operative patients may have minimal pain. Grey Turner/Cullen ecchymosis is rare (3% in one large series) and marks severity rather than aiding diagnosis.
ask.positive_finding: Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back with an alcohol or gallstone history is the classic presentation of acute pancreatitis and is one of the three diagnostic criteria in the revised Atlanta classification (with lipase/amylase >3x ULN and imaging). The same pain pattern also occurs with posterior penetrating peptic ulcer, ruptured AAA and aortic dissection.
ask.prerequisites: Reliable history; ask family when the patient is intoxicated or encephalopathic.
ask.title: Constant epigastric pain radiating to the back (with alcohol/gallstone history)

ask.changes_what: Shaking chills should prompt blood cultures and a search for a bacteremic source (line, biliary, urinary, endovascular); no chills supports withholding cultures when pretest probability is low.
ask.do_not_use_when: The RCE conclusions do not apply to immunocompromised patients or when endocarditis is suspected; in those groups obtain cultures regardless of chills.
ask.escalation_warning: Rigors with hypotension, altered mentation or a central line indicate probable bacteremia/sepsis: cultures, source control and antibiotics within the hour.

evidence.citation: Coburn B, Morris AM, Tomlinson G, Detsky AS. Does this adult patient with suspected bacteremia require blood cultures? JAMA. 2012;308(5):502-511.
evidence.population: Adult immunocompetent patients in whom bacteremia was suspected (35 studies; 4566 bacteremia and 25,946 negative episodes)
evidence.quote: The severity of chills graded on an ordinal scale (shaking chills, LR, 4.7; 95% CI, 3.0-7.2) may be more useful.

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: Shaking chills showed a specificity of 90.3% (95% CI 89.2-91.5) and positive likelihood ratio of 4.65 (95% CI 2.95-6.86).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: shaking chills (whole-body shaking under a thick blanket)

evidence.citation: Tokuda Y, Miyasato H, Stein GH, Kishaba T. The degree of chills for risk of bacteremia in acute febrile illness. Am J Med. 2005;118(12):1417.
evidence.population: 526 consecutive adults with acute febrile illness (40, 7.6%, bacteremic)
evidence.quote: The absence of chills showed a sensitivity of 87.5% (95% CI 74.4-94.5) and negative likelihood ratio of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11-0.51).
evidence.target_condition: Bacteremia - finding: any chills (sensitivity and LR- refer to absence of chills)

ask.how: Ask the patient (or witnesses) whether they have had chills and grade the worst episode: mild = feeling cold, needing a jacket; moderate = needing a thick blanket; shaking chills = whole-body shaking even under a thick blanket. Record timing relative to fever and any line, procedure or infusion.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of any chills lowers the probability of bacteremia (LR- 0.24) but does not exclude it, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients who may not mount rigors.
ask.pitfalls: Rigors also occur with malaria, transfusion or drug reactions, and after amphotericin or contaminated infusions; the grading relies on patient recall and the RCE data exclude immunocompromised patients and suspected endocarditis.
ask.positive_finding: Shaking (rigor-grade) chills raise the probability of bacteremia about 4.7-fold (LR+ 4.7, 95% CI 3.0-7.2; specificity 0.90) and justify blood cultures before antibiotics.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or witness able to describe the episode; ask before antipyretics blunt recall.
ask.title: Rigors / shaking chills

examine.changes_what: Positive: escalate to imaging and surgical review for suspected appendicitis/peritonitis; negative in low-risk patients supports observation, not discharge without follow-up.
examine.contraindications: Avoid in an already rigid, obviously peritonitic abdomen where the manoeuvre adds only pain; prefer percussion or cough tenderness.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use a negative result to exclude peritonitis in elderly, immunosuppressed, steroid-treated, obese or obtunded patients, or in pregnancy where the appendix is displaced.
examine.escalation_warning: Generalised rebound with fever, tachycardia or hypotension indicates diffuse peritonitis: resuscitate and obtain immediate surgical review.

evidence.citation: Golledge J, Toms AP, Franklin IJ, Scriven MW, Galland RB. Assessment of peritonism in appendicitis. Ann R Coll Surg Engl. 1996;78(1):11-14.
evidence.population: 100 consecutive patients with right iliac fossa pain, median age 25 (range 4-81), UK surgical unit; 44 histology-proven appendicitis
evidence.quote: Rebound tenderness proved to be sensitive (sensitivity 0.82), specific (specificity 0.89) and accurate (accuracy 86%).
evidence.reference_standard: Histology at operation; non-operated patients followed clinically

evidence.citation: Bundy DG, Byerley JS, Liles EA, Perrin EM, Katznelson J, Rice HE. Does this child have appendicitis? JAMA. 2007;298(4):438-451.
evidence.population: Children <=18 years in whom appendicitis was suspected and evaluation undertaken; pooled from quality level >=3 studies
evidence.quote: rebound tenderness triples the odds of appendicitis (summary LR, 3.0; 95% CI, 2.3-3.9), while its absence reduces the likelihood (summary LR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.14-0.55)
evidence.reference_standard: Surgical pathology, clinical observation or follow-up

examine.how: Press slowly and deeply with the fingertips over the area of concern (or a remote quadrant), hold, then release abruptly while watching the patient's face. Pain on release greater than on pressure is rebound tenderness. Gentler equivalents: percussion tenderness, or pain on coughing or heel-drop.
examine.negative_finding: Absence lowers the probability of appendicitis (pediatric LR- 0.28) but does not exclude early, retrocaecal or pelvic appendicitis or peritonitis in the elderly and immunosuppressed.
examine.pitfalls: The classic release manoeuvre is painful and non-specific in anxious patients; percussion or cough tenderness gives similar information more gently. False negatives occur with steroids, advanced age, obesity and altered mental status.
examine.positive_finding: Rebound (or percussion/cough) tenderness indicates parietal peritoneal inflammation; in RIF pain it is specific for appendicitis (spec 0.89, sens 0.82 in adults; pediatric LR+ 3.0).
examine.prerequisites: Explain the manoeuvre; give analgesia first (it does not abolish peritoneal signs); perform once, not repeatedly.
examine.title: Rebound tenderness (peritoneal irritation)

examine.changes_what: Isolated LLQ tenderness + no vomiting + CRP>50: diverticulitis likely; consider CT to stage. Diffuse tenderness/peritonism or incomplete features: CT to exclude perforation, abscess or alternatives.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a benign LLQ exam in immunosuppressed, steroid-treated or very elderly patients, in whom perforation can present with minimal tenderness.
examine.escalation_warning: Diffuse peritonism, rigidity, hypotension or a tender mass suggests perforation or abscess: urgent CT and surgical review.

evidence.citation: Laméris W, van Randen A, van Gulik TM et al. A clinical decision rule to establish the diagnosis of acute diverticulitis at the emergency department. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2010.
evidence.population: 126 ED patients with acute abdominal pain and clinically suspected diverticulitis before imaging (80 with final diagnosis of diverticulitis), from a prospective cohort of 1,021 ED abdominal-pain patients, Netherlands
evidence.quote: 30 patients had all 3 features (24%), of whom 29 had a final diagnosis of acute diverticulitis (97%; 95% CI: 83%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis by expert panel after imaging and follow-up
evidence.target_condition: COMPOSITE: direct tenderness only in the LLQ AND absence of vomiting AND CRP >50 mg/L (Lameris rule, all three present) for final diagnosis of acute diverticulitis

evidence.citation: Laurell H, Hansson LE, Gunnarsson U. Acute diverticulitis--clinical presentation and differential diagnostics. Colorectal disease : the official journal of the Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland. 2007.
evidence.population: 3,349 patients admitted with abdominal pain of up to 7 days' duration, prospectively registered, Swedish hospital (145 with final diagnosis of diverticulitis)
evidence.quote: Sensitivity of diverticulitis as primary diagnosis was 64% and specificity 97%.
evidence.target_condition: Clinician's primary (admission) diagnosis of acute diverticulitis - overall clinical gestalt including LLQ tenderness, NOT the isolated sign

examine.how: Palpate all four quadrants, leaving the painful area until last; record whether direct tenderness is confined to the left lower quadrant (versus diffuse or elsewhere), and whether there is guarding, rebound or a palpable mass. Ask specifically about previous confirmed episodes of diverticulitis and about vomiting.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of isolated LLQ tenderness does not exclude diverticulitis (the three-feature rule captured only about one-third of confirmed cases); clinicians' overall clinical diagnosis has a sensitivity of roughly 0.64 with a high false-positive rate, so imaging (CT) is needed when features are incomplete.
examine.pitfalls: Redundant sigmoid, right-sided diverticulitis (more common in Asian patients) and elderly or immunosuppressed patients give atypical locations or minimal tenderness. Diffuse tenderness, rigidity or peritonism signals perforation or abscess, not uncomplicated diverticulitis.
examine.positive_finding: Tenderness confined to the LLQ, especially with a prior episode, no vomiting and CRP >50 mg/L, makes acute diverticulitis very likely (PPV 97% for the three-feature rule in clinically suspected patients), and can allow treatment without imaging in uncomplicated cases in some pathways.
examine.prerequisites: Patient supine and relaxed; analgesia does not preclude examination.
examine.title: Localized LLQ tenderness (with prior diverticulitis episode history)

examine.changes_what: Localised RLQ tenderness plus migration/rebound/fever: image (US/CT) or surgical review; absent tenderness in a well patient supports observation with re-examination.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of McBurney tenderness to exclude appendicitis in pregnancy, the elderly, or when symptoms are <12 h old.
examine.escalation_warning: RLQ tenderness with rigidity, fever and tachycardia suggests perforation: urgent surgical review and CT.
examine.how: Palpate the right lower quadrant at McBurney point (one-third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus) with gentle then deeper pressure, watching the patient's face. Note maximal tenderness there compared with the other quadrants; check for Rovsing sign (RLQ pain on LLQ pressure), psoas and obturator signs.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of RLQ tenderness makes appendicitis less likely (RCE 1996) but does not exclude retrocaecal, pelvic or early appendicitis, or appendicitis in pregnancy where the point of tenderness shifts.
examine.pitfalls: RLQ tenderness is common in many conditions (mesenteric adenitis, ovarian pathology, caecal diverticulitis, Crohn disease), so specificity is limited; the appendix position varies, so tenderness may be elsewhere.
examine.positive_finding: Isolated, well-localised RIF/McBurney tenderness had the highest odds ratio for appendicitis (OR 3.29) among examination findings in an adult ED cohort; combined with guarding or rebound it strongly supports the diagnosis.
examine.prerequisites: Supine, relaxed patient; examine painful area last; analgesia does not abolish localised tenderness.
examine.title: RLQ (McBurney point) tenderness

examine.changes_what: Present: treat as peritonitis, obtain surgical review and CT urgently. Absent: modest reassurance only; do not use to withhold imaging.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid deep or repeated palpation once peritonitis is evident.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on absence of guarding to exclude surgical pathology in the elderly, immunosuppressed, obese, pregnant or opioid-treated patient.
examine.escalation_warning: Diffuse rigidity with hypotension or fever is generalized peritonitis until proven otherwise: resuscitate, antibiotics, immediate surgical consultation.

evidence.citation: Becker T, Kharbanda A, Bachur R. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
evidence.population: 755 children and adolescents (median age 11.9 y) evaluated for suspected appendicitis; 36% had appendicitis
evidence.target_condition: Acute appendicitis (absence of guarding as negative predictor) (pediatric)

evidence.citation: Becker T, Kharbanda A, Bachur R. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
evidence.population: Children and adolescents with proven appendicitis in the same cohort (n=755 enrolled)

examine.how: With the patient supine, knees flexed and distracted by conversation, palpate each quadrant gently with a flat hand. Involuntary guarding is reflex contraction of the abdominal wall that persists despite relaxation and distraction; rigidity is a board-like wall that does not soften on expiration.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of guarding lowers but does not exclude appendicitis (pediatric LR- ~0.6); early, retrocaecal or perforated disease in the elderly or immunosuppressed may show no guarding.
examine.pitfalls: Voluntary guarding from anxiety, cold hands or ticklishness mimics the sign; obesity, steroids, opioids and advanced age blunt it. Distinguishing voluntary from involuntary guarding is examiner dependent.
examine.positive_finding: Involuntary guarding or rigidity indicates parietal peritoneal irritation (localized or generalized peritonitis) and raises the probability of appendicitis, perforation or other surgical pathology.
examine.prerequisites: Patient able to lie supine and relax; warm hands; examine tender areas last.
examine.title: Involuntary guarding / board-like rigidity
